searchText: I see that's why I added the "MAY queue" to assess the shuffling instead of MUST. This leaves the client able to make a decision on if it's worth investigating (e.g. might be if just a singular instance, but might not be if you just got flooded with weird looking fork blocks). But I see your point, limiting scope of attack to a reduced set (validators) does seem like the right way to go. A malicious set of validators could then attempt to DoS you with N blocks. You would verify the sigs and then if you decided to go investigate the past states, it would be costly but these messages wouldn't make it far in the gossip. I think "MAY queue" is still correct here to reduce the required workload when under this type of attack because otherwise, a set of N validators has an N-1 allowance per slot to get you to lookup past states. > I think "MAY queue" is still correct here to reduce the required workload when under this type of attack because otherwise, a set of N validators has an N-1 allowance per slot to get you to lookup past states. <@!291925846556540928> so the MAY here means that we don't necessarily have to check the shuffling before gossiping? Or do you queue, check shuffling then publish? MAY is in reference to queuing and coming back to it for potential gossip otherwise the condition would fail and you drop Gives optionality in investigating some weird fork blocks but not requiring to do it for all Especially considering a cartel of N validators have an allowance of at least N-1 valid looking sigs per slot Cool, thanks. What's a valid-looking sig? Oh a signature for a slot where you're not a proposer? yeah sorry, a block made by some random validator beacuse slashing is making two of those blocks per slot, anyone not assigned to a slot can make a block with a valid sig you could then point to some old block (say last epoch or the one before) as the parent even if the resulting shuffling doesn't dictate that that validator is the proposer at the slot on that fork but you'd have to go dig it up to know for sure i feel you, this is what my nightmares consist of 😛 "noooo reading old states from the database" yup. such slow, many allocation if you locally are seeing tons of attestations on some good looking blocks, might not be worth your time Or if you only see one of these come in from time to time, might be worth your time but if you get a ton (especially for same slot), red flag, dos, drop most of them

excerpts.author: djrtwo
excerpts.content:
I see
that's why I added the "MAY queue" to assess the shuffling instead of MUST. This leaves the client able to make a decision on if it's worth investigating (e.g. might be if just a singular instance, but might not be if you just got flooded with weird looking fork blocks). 

But I see your point, limiting scope of attack to a reduced set (validators) does  seem like the right way to go. 

A malicious set of validators could then attempt to DoS you with N blocks. You would verify the sigs and then if you decided to go investigate the past states, it would be costly but these messages wouldn't make it far in the gossip. I think "MAY queue" is still correct here to reduce the required workload when under this type of attack because otherwise, a set of N validators has an N-1 allowance per slot to get you to lookup past states.

excerpts.author: paulhauner
excerpts.content:
> I think "MAY queue" is still correct here to reduce the required workload when under this type of attack because otherwise, a set of N validators has an N-1 allowance per slot to get you to lookup past states.
<@!291925846556540928> so the MAY here means that we don't necessarily have to check the shuffling before gossiping? Or do you queue, check shuffling then publish?

excerpts.author: djrtwo
excerpts.content: MAY is in reference to queuing and coming back to it for potential gossip

excerpts.author: djrtwo
excerpts.content: otherwise the condition would fail and you drop

excerpts.author: djrtwo
excerpts.content: Gives optionality in investigating some weird fork blocks but not requiring to do it for all

excerpts.author: djrtwo
excerpts.content: Especially considering a cartel of N validators have an allowance of at least N-1 valid looking sigs per slot

excerpts.author: paulhauner
excerpts.content: Cool, thanks. What's a valid-looking sig?

excerpts.author: paulhauner
excerpts.content: Oh a signature for a slot where you're not a proposer?

excerpts.author: djrtwo
excerpts.content: yeah sorry, a block made by some random validator

excerpts.author: djrtwo
excerpts.content: beacuse slashing is making two of those blocks per slot, anyone not assigned to a slot can make a block with a valid sig

excerpts.author: djrtwo
excerpts.content: you could then point to some old block (say last epoch or the one before) as the parent even if the resulting shuffling doesn't dictate that that validator is the proposer at the slot on that fork

excerpts.author: djrtwo
excerpts.content: but you'd have to go dig it up to know for sure
